summaries.summary: Public debates juxtapose diverging viewpoints and, unlike monologues, let participants interactively attack opponents' points while defending their own, making idea flow key.
This work introduces a computational framework characterizing debates by conversational flow, tracking promoting one's own points and attacking opponents' points to predict audience persuasion.
Oxford-style debates provide a convenient setting for studying conversational flow because two teams persuade a live audience whose votes before and after determine the winner.
The debate format's opening statements identify participants' prior talking points separately from points introduced spontaneously during discussion.
This work introduces a debate dataset with rich metadata, proposes a framework for tracking idea flow, and shows its effectiveness in a predictive setting.
The study uses transcripts and results from “Intelligence Squared Debates” (IQ2), Oxford-style debates with two opposing teams, a moderator, and three rounds.
The dataset contains transcripts of all IQ2 US debates from September 2006 up to September 2015, totaling 108 debates averaging 12801 words in 117 turns.
Winning side labels follow IQ2's criteria using pre- and post-debate audience votes, with the larger “delta” winning; for 30% of debates, delta differences are less than 10%.
Audience feedback checks voting results using laughter and applause, finding winning teams receive more laughter during discussion and more applause during conclusion.
The running example is the “Millennials don't stand a chance” debate, where the For side won with a delta of 20% versus the Against side's 5%.
Promoting one's own points and addressing the opponent's points are two primary debating strategies, and this methodology identifies them to investigate usage and outcome effects.

Talking points are identified from introduction words whose usage differs significantly between teams using monroe2008fightin, multinomial distributions, a uniform Dirichlet prior, log-odds ratio, and z-scores.
The flow of talking points quantifies strategies by comparing airtime through self-coverage and opponent-coverage fractions of content words in each round.
Self-coverage dominates during discussion, but interaction causes a sharp drop in self-coverage and a rise in opponent-coverage once discussion begins.
Figure FIGREF11 suggests strategic advantages because winning sides show slightly larger drops in self-coverage and in the sum of self- and opponent-coverage.
Discussion points are words introduced during discussion and adopted by opponents at least twice; only 3% of newly introduced words qualify, about 10 discussion points per debate.
During discussion, eventual winners adopt more opponent-introduced discussion points than eventual losers, raising topic control and contesting interpretations.
A post-hoc manual examination supports contesting opponents' points: 78% of valid discussion points are picked up to be challenged, suggesting winners engage more with opponents' ideas.
Predictive power is evaluated in binary classification predicting whether the For or Against side wins, aiming to understand which developed flow features carry predictive power.
Flow features include conversational features for each side, their sum, the drop in self-coverage, and the number of discussion points adopted by each side.
Baseline features use number of words uttered and number of turns taken by each side (length), plus a unigram baseline (BOW), to test debater verbosity.
Audience features use counts of applause and laughter received by each side as rough indicators of how well the audience can foresee a debate's outcome.
Prediction accuracy uses leave-one-out (LOO), logistic regression, 3-fold cross-validation, and univariate feature selection on flow features in the Flow* setting.
Conversation flow features obtain the best accuracy (Flow: 63%; Flow*: 65%), above a 50% random baseline and comparable to audience features (60%), while length and BOW do not beat chance.

Flow* most often selects number of discussion points adopted, recall of talking points during discussion, and drop in usage of own talking points, suggesting audiences favor discussion-emphasizing strategies.
Previous work modeled dialogue acts, interleaved conversations, conversation-level traits, and participant-level stances, while known debate stances and turn structure let this work focus on outcome.
Existing argumentation strategy research focused on monologic arguments and forum challenges; this work complements it by examining relative persuasiveness in extended multi-turn conversations.
Previous influence studies in extended conversations examined political talk shows or presidential debates; this work extends them to idea flow in a highly structured setting controlling confounds.

Future research could use topic models or word embeddings, add speakers' linguistic choices, compare monologic and interactive dynamics, and clarify strategic implications of dialogue versus self-promotion.
Simplifying assumptions include a basic unigram-based definition of discussion points that ignores context or semantic sense, with annotators finding many referred to differing ideas.
The Oxford-style debate dataset is limited in size, and future work could examine flow features in settings like Wikipedia talk pages, education, and cooperative work.
Acknowledgements thank reviewers, V. Niculae, I. Arawjo, and D. Sedra, and note support in part by a Google Faculty Research Award.
